extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of law, political philosophy, and legal theory (readers of Hobbes/Leviathan)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and applies Hobbesian criteria for what counts as a crime, what excuses or attenuates culpability, how crimes are graded, and what properly counts as punishment by public authority. Useful for analyzing wrongdoing, culpability, and lawful punishment in early-modern political theory and legal philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt includes acts, words, omissions, and intentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Contempt (a breach of the sovereign's laws) may consist not only in commission of forbidden acts or speaking forbidden words, or omission of commanded acts, but also in the intention or purpose to transgress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that intention or purpose to break the law is itself a degree of contempt; however, mere pleasure in imagining forbidden things (e.g., coveting in fantasy) without resolving to act is not the breach the civil law would punish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime vs. Sin: outward appearance required for crime
rubrics_metrics.description: A Crime is a sin consisting in the committing (by deed or word) of that which the Law forbids, or omission of what it commands; every Crime is a sin, but not every sin a Crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentions that never appear by outward act are sins in the sight of God but are not subject to human accusation or civil crime. The distinction is exemplified by Greek and Latin terms (amartema/peccatum for sin; egklema/crimen for crimes perceptible before a judge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Where civil law ceases, crime ceases (but natural law remains sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: If civil law ceases to exist, crimes (as subjects of human accusation) cease; violations contrary to natural law remain sins but not civil crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sovereign power has ended or been removed, there may be no protection from law and hence no civil accusation; only conscience and natural law remain applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of the law of nature excuses no man
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of the Law of Nature excuseth no man because every reasonable person is supposed to know he ought not to do to another what he would not have done to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus actions contrary to the law of nature are crimes in any place; e.g., introducing doctrines that tend to disobedience to a country's laws may be punished even if sincerely believed true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of civil law may sometimes excuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of the civil law of a man's own country may excuse when the law is not sufficiently declared so that he could know it; ignorance of civil law in a strange country excuses until it is declared to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of means to know a law (not lack of diligence) can be a total excuse; but mere negligence to inquire is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of the sovereign excuses not
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of the sovereign power in one's ordinary residence does not excuse because one ought to take notice of the power that protects him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizens are presumed to be aware of the sovereign authority that governs their ordinary residence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of the penalty excuses not
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of the penalty, where the law is declared, excuses no man: punishment is a known consequence of violating laws and is accepted when one voluntarily acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If penalty is determined by law, the offender is subject to it even if unaware; if no penalty is prescribed, arbitrary punishment may follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declared punishments before the fact limit later punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: When a penalty is annexed to the crime in the law or has been usually inflicted, the delinquent is excused from a greater punishment imposed afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreknown, insufficiently severe punishments may invite offense; imposing a greater punishment after the fact is treating the lawmaker as tempting and deceiving the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: No ex post facto laws: cannot make past acts crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: No law made after a fact done can make it a crime; a positive law cannot be obligatory retroactively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the law forbidding the act was in place before the act, the actor is liable to the penalties then known; otherwise ex post facto criminalization is invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: False principles and authorities cause crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Erroneous reasoning or acceptance of false principles (e.g., equating success with rightness, following examples of powerful wrongdoers) can lead people to think actions are not crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns against adopting as principles the practices of winners or the common practices of nations; such false principles undermine recognition of injustice and promote crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: False teachers and misinterpretation of natural law
rubrics_metrics.description: False teachers who misinterpret the law of nature or teach doctrines/traditions inconsistent with duty to the sovereign foster crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors arising from publicly-authorized teachers are treated differently (see 'Evill Teachers, Extenuate').

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous inferences from true principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Hasty or precipitate reasoning, where men draw false inferences from true principles without study, leads to criminal actions and is a poor excuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who hold public charge or govern themselves are expected to have sufficient study and prudence; such errors may at best extenuate, not excuse, crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions (vain-glory, presumption of riches/friends, false wisdom) cause and aggravate crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Vain-glory, presumption that wealth or connections will shield one, and overestimation of one's own wisdom incline persons to commit crimes and to think they are exempt from punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These passions produce readiness to offend (e.g., corruption of justice, seeking pardon by money) and often co-occur with anger, making violent crimes more likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hatred, lust, ambition, covetousness are common causes of crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Hatred, lust, ambition, and covetousness readily produce crimes; they are natural infirmities that require extraordinary reason or constant severity in punishment to be restrained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because these passions are persistent or vehement, they overcome reason when hope of impunity appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear justifies only immediate bodily danger
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear sometimes causes crime and may justify action only where the danger is present and corporeal; speculative, phantom, or social fears do not excuse criminal acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Killing in immediate self-defense is not a crime; killing to avoid a feared future harm that could be addressed through sovereign protection is a crime. Belief in dreams/visions or superstition does not excuse breaking law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crimes are not equal — scope for excuse and extenuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Crimes differ in degree; there is room for total excuse (removing the nature of a crime) and for extenuation (making a great crime less), so not all crimes are equally unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison is like crooked lines: all deviate from rectitude but to different extents; law should reflect degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total excuses that remove crime
rubrics_metrics.description: A total excuse takes away the obligation of the law and therefore removes the nature of a crime; such excuses include want of means to know the law, infancy/madness, captivity/enemy compulsion (without fault), present terror of death, and necessity to preserve life (e.g., taking food in famine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Want of diligence is not want of means. Acts done under enemy compulsion or to avoid immediate death are totally excused as the obligation of law ceases in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority/execution excuses the actor from the author (but not the injured third party)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts done by authority of another are excused as regards the author (one should not accuse his own instrument), though both author and actor are criminal as to the injured third party; sovereign commands contrary to a former law excuse obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sovereign or assembly commands what contradicts a former law, doing it is excused toward the author because the sovereign cannot justly condemn his own command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of crime measured on four scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Degrees of crime are measured (1) by malignity of the source or cause, (2) by contagion of the example, (3) by mischief of the effect, and (4) by concurrence of times, places, and persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four dimensions guide how severely the law should treat a given criminal act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of power (impunity) aggravates crime
rubrics_metrics.description: If the same act proceeds from presumption of strength, riches, or friends (hope of resisting law execution), it is a greater crime than if it proceeded from hope of escape or concealment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumption of impunity is a root cause of contempt of laws and promotes recidivism; crimes done despite one's conscience (presuming power) are worse than those done in error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evill (public) teachers' authority extenuates error
rubrics_metrics.description: Errour deriving from authority of a public teacher or interpreter of law is less blameworthy than error from private, peremptory pursuit of one's own principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly taught doctrines resemble law until overruled; such errors may totally excuse where they do not deny sovereign power or breach evident law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of impunity extenuate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there have been many precedent examples of impunity, the same fact committed is less culpable because the sovereign has partly furnished hope of impunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedents of lenient enforcement distribute part of the fault to those who set the example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premeditation aggravates; sudden passion may extenuate but not totally excuse
rubrics_metrics.description: A crime arising from long meditation is greater than one arising from sudden passion; sudden passion can mitigate but does not totally excuse because time between knowing the law and acting counts as deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of public instruction about the law increases culpability for deliberate transgressions; lack of public instruction partly discharges fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tacit approbation by sovereign extenuates
rubrics_metrics.description: If the law condemns a fact but the lawmaker tacitly approves it by other signs, the fact is a lesser crime than if condemned both by law and lawmaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign example influences subjects; where sovereign behavior contradicts formal prohibition, blame is partly discharged on the punisher for mixed signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of crimes by effect: harm to many, future harm, and scandal
rubrics_metrics.description: A crime that harms many, that causes future or multiplying harm (fertile crime), or that scandalizes and leads the weak to imitate, is greater than a crime that harms few or has only present effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offenses by persons of reputation (preachers, professors, wise men) are graver because they teach or model law-breaking to many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crimes against the commonwealth (laesae majestas) are greater
rubrics_metrics.description: Hostile acts against the state — betraying strongholds, revealing secrets, attempts on the representative (monarch or assembly), or words/deeds diminishing authority — are greater crimes (crimina laesae majestatis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such acts injure all and threaten the fundamental law/peace of the commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crimes that render judgments ineffective are especially grave
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiving money to give false judgement or testimony is a greater crime because it makes all judgments useless and invites force and private revenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corruption of judicial process damages the commonwealth more than ordinary private wrongs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embezzlement/robbery of public treasure is more serious
rubrics_metrics.description: Robbery or embezzlement of public treasure (revenues) is a greater crime than robbing a private man, because it robs many at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misappropriation of public funds undermines the commonwealth and affects many citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfeiting public authority aggravates crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterfeiting public ministry, public seals, or public coin is worse than counterfeiting a private man's person or seal because its fraud damages many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterfeiting instruments of the state spreads harm widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking private harms: killing, torture, mutilation, robbery, deception, sexual violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Among private offences: killing is greater than other injuries; killing with torment greater than simple killing; mutilation of a limb greater than spoiling goods; spoiling goods by terror greater than clandestine theft; clandestine theft greater than fraud by consent; rape by force greater than rape by flattery; rape of a married woman greater than of an unmarried one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rankings reflect common valuation and indicate how law should distinguish degrees of private wrongs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors: person, time, and place
rubrics_metrics.description: Crimes are aggravated by the person (e.g., killing one's parent worse), by victim's vulnerability (robbing the poor is worse), and by time/place (crimes in places/times of devotion are worse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law considers the social and relational context: offenses against parents, in sacred times/places, or against the poor merit greater censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between public and private pleas/crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: When accusation is in the name of the commonwealth, it is a public crime (judicia publica); when in the name of a private man, a private crime and plea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same underlying act may be prosecuted as private or public depending on who brings the accusation; the public plea addresses commonwealth injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: "A PUNISHMENT, is an Evill inflicted by publique Authority, on him that hath done, or omitted that which is Judged by the same Authority to be a Transgression of the Law; to the end that the will of men may thereby the better be disposed to obedience."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment's purpose is the future disposition of will to obey law; it must be inflicted by public authority upon a judged transgression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to punish derived from natural right preserved in commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The right or authority of punishing in the commonwealth is not grounded on concession of subjects but derives from the pre-institution right to preserve oneself; subjects strengthened the sovereign to use that right for preservation of all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign punishment is thus as entire as the original natural right to punish, limited only by natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private injuries and private revenge are not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Private revenges or injuries by private men are not 'punishment' because they do not proceed from public authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment requires public authorization/condemnation and aims at future obedience, not mere private injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of preferment is not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Being neglected or unpreferred by public favor is not punishment because it does not inflict a new evil; it leaves one in the previous estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment must be an inflicted evil, not mere omission of reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain inflicted without public hearing is not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evil inflicted by public authority without prior public condemnation is not 'punishment' but an act of hostility; punishment must be preceded by public judgment that the act was a transgression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process/public condemnation is intrinsic to proper punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain inflicted by usurped power is not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Hurt inflicted by usurped power or judges without authority is not punishment but hostile action because usurped acts have no legitimate authorizing sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimacy of authority is a prerequisite for lawful punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain inflicted without reference to future good is not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Any evil inflicted without intention or possibility of disposing the delinquent (or others by example) to obey the laws is an act of hostility, not punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The telos of punishment is future obedience; if absent, the act cannot be classed as punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural evil consequences are not human punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Harm that naturally follows certain actions (e.g., being slain while assaulting) is a divine, natural consequence but not 'punishment' in the human sense because it is not inflicted by human authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only evils inflicted by public authority with the aim of reform/deterrence are punishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm less than the benefit of transgression is not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the harm inflicted is less than the benefit or satisfaction gained by committing the crime, that harm is not punishment but rather the price or redemption for the act, failing the aim of inducing obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment must be sufficiently deterrent relative to the perceived benefit of the crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excess punishment beyond what law prescribes is hostility, not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: If a punishment is prescribed by law and after the crime a greater punishment is inflicted, the excess is not punishment but an act of hostility; where no prior punishment is determined by law, what is inflicted is punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retroactive escalation of penalties is illegitimate; declared penalties before the fact bound subsequent enforcement.
